A model of a particular setting needs data about its people and its places: how many people there are and of what ages, how fast they are born and die, who has contact with whom, and where they live. Starsim has these for 187 countries and territories, by name, and takes data of your own in the same forms. This page covers the data that comes with Starsim and using data of your own, and then places: a model split into places, geographies of towns or of a country's administrative units, maps of results, and values by place. Places work the same under compartments and agents.

These data describe a setting; they don't set the disease's parameters, and a model that uses them still needs checking against data on the disease itself (see [Fitting a model](calibration_fitting.qmd)). How a population, its births, and its deaths are used is in [People and demographics](populations_people.qmd), and contact matrices and movement between places in [Mixing](populations_mixing.qmd). The tutorial [T4 – Mixing](../tutorials/t4_mixing.qmd) builds up a model of several towns step by step, and [T6 – Data and calibration](../tutorials/t6_data.qmd) uses real places and populations; this page is for looking things up.

## Data by place

The data by place comes from the package `starsim_data`: populations by age and sex, rates of birth, death, fertility, and migration, contact matrices, and administrative units (counties, provinces, and states). Coverage differs by dataset: the UN's demographic data is there for 187 countries and territories, the default contact matrices for 177 of them, and the first-level administrative units for 184. What is small and common is bundled with the package, so it needs no download: the UN data, the contact matrices of Prem et al., and administrative units at levels 0 (the country) and 1 (its counties, provinces, or states). The rest (the units at level 2, populations for another year, and the other contact matrices) is downloaded on first use and kept in a cache. Which places have which data is in the [appendix](#appendix-every-place-and-its-data). The model objects that use a place take its name, and `ss.data` gives the data itself, for looking at or using elsewhere:

| What | In a model | The data itself |
|---|---|---|
| Population by age and sex (UN World Population Prospects) | `ss.population('Kenya')` | `ss.data.population('Kenya')`, `ss.data.age('Kenya')` |
| Contact matrix by 5-year age group (Prem et al. 2021) | `ss.contacts('Kenya')` | `ss.data.contacts('Kenya')` |
| Birth and death rates by year (and by age and sex, for deaths) | `ss.Births(birth_rate='Kenya')`, `ss.Deaths(death_rate='Kenya')` | `ss.data.rates('Kenya', 'births')`, `ss.data.rates('Kenya', 'deaths')` |
| Fertility rates by year and 5-year age group of the mother | `ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate='Kenya')` | `ss.data.rates('Kenya', 'fertility')` |
| Net migration rates by year | `ss.migration(rate='Kenya')` (see [Migration](populations_people.qmd#migration)) | `ss.data.rates('Kenya', 'migration')` |
| Administrative units, with their populations and positions | `ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1)` | `ss.data.geography('Kenya', level=1)` |

A named population gives the sim its size (`total_pop`) and the share of people in each age group, so a model stratified by age needs no shares of its own; as agents, it gives the agents their ages and sex (see [Ages and sex](populations_people.qmd#ages-and-sex)). Birth and death rates are in [People and demographics](populations_people.qmd#rates-from-data), contact matrices in [Mixing](populations_mixing.qmd#contact-matrices-by-setting), and administrative units [below](#geographies).

`ss.population()` takes a year, and `ss.contacts()` a study: `ss.population('Kenya', year=2030)` (from 1950 to 2100, with the years between the UN's decadal values interpolated), and `ss.contacts('Japan', study='mistry2021')` for the matrices of Mistry et al. (2021), by single year of age, for 36 countries (the sources are listed in the [appendix](#appendix-every-dataset)). A US state is named with its country, `ss.population('United States:Massachusetts')` and `ss.contacts('United States:Massachusetts')`, from the US Census and Mistry et al. The data is given as tables (dataframes), with the age groups labeled as a stratification by age labels them (`'0-4'`, `'5-9'`, ..., `'100+'`) and where the data came from in `.attrs['ref']`:

```{python}
import starsim as ss

births = ss.data.rates('Kenya', 'births') # Crude birth rates per 1,000 people, by year
print(births.head())

pop = ss.data.population('Kenya', year=2024) # Women and men by 5-year age group
print(pop.head())
print('Population of Kenya in 2024:', round(pop.values.sum()))
print('Source:', pop.attrs['ref']['study'])
```

Every piece of data records where it came from, which `describe()` shows. Record the source and year with an analysis: the data don't all have the same reference year.

### Looking up a place

A place can be named in several ways: by its name (`'Kenya'`), its ISO code (`'KE'` or `'KEN'`), its official name, or a common alias (`'Czechia'` for the Czech Republic), without regard to case or accents. `starsim_data` can say what it has for a place, and plot it as a check before it goes into a model, here an age pyramid, the crude birth rate over time, death rates by age, and the contact matrix:

```{python}
import starsim_data as ssd

info = ssd.location_info('KEN') # The name, codes, aliases, and sources of the contact matrices
print(info.location, info.iso3, info.official_name, '- contact matrices:', info.contact_sources)
print('Places with a contact matrix of Prem et al. 2021:', len(ssd.list_locations('prem2021')))
ssd.plot('Kenya');
```

`ssd.list_locations(dataset)` lists the places in a dataset, and `ssd.list_datasets(detailed=True)` the datasets, as in the appendices below. The data that is downloaded is kept in a cache (`ssd.cache_dir()`; `ssd.cache_info()` lists what is in it), so it is downloaded once; on a computer with no connection to the internet, a dataset that is not bundled or already in the cache raises a `ConnectionError` that says so.

The UN's net migration rates (`ss.data.rates('Kenya', 'migration')`, per 1,000 people a year, positive for more people arriving than leaving) are part of the UN's estimates of the population, so a model with births and deaths but no migration drifts from the UN's totals where migration is large. [Migration](populations_people.qmd#migration) shows how to use them.

## Data of your own

Data of your own takes the same forms as the data by place. Ages are a table of counts or shares by age group, for `ss.People(n_agents, age_data=...)` (see [Ages and sex](populations_people.qmd#ages-and-sex)), and `ss.data.age()` gives a country's in that form, for a different year or to change before use:

```{python}
ppl = ss.People(10_000, age_data=ss.data.age('Kenya', year=2000))
```

For data by 5-year age group and a model with other age groups, `ss.data.age_split(edges, ages, counts)` gives the share of people in each of the model's groups (with ages spread evenly within each 5-year group), and `ss.data.age_labels(edges)` labels groups as Starsim does (`'0-14'`, `'15-64'`, `'65+'`).

Birth and death rates are tables by year (and by sex and age for deaths), for `ss.Births()` and `ss.Deaths()` (see [Data of your own](populations_people.qmd#data-of-your-own) in People and demographics); a contact matrix is an array, with the lower edges of its age groups, for `ss.contacts(matrix, ages=...)` (see [The forms of a matrix](populations_mixing.qmd#the-forms-of-a-matrix)), or a table labeled by age group (`'0-14'`, `'15-64'`, `'65+'`), as `ss.data.contacts()` gives, for `ss.contacts(table)`; and places are a table of names, populations, and positions, for `ss.geo.geography()` (see [Geographies](#geographies)).

Data on the disease itself (cases, deaths, prevalence) is a different input: it is given to the sim with `data=`, to plot with the results and fit the model to (see [Fitting a model](calibration_fitting.qmd)). Before using any data, check its units, its denominators, and the period it covers: a contact survey gives contacts a day, a crude birth rate is per 1,000 people a year, and a blank cell means not observed, while a zero is a count of none.

## Towns linked by commuting

A **geography** (`ss.geo.geography`) is a set of named places, with the population of each and where they are. Stratifying a disease by it (`stratify(patch=towns)`) makes a copy of each state for each place, and `mobility=` says how people move between them (see [Movement between places](populations_mixing.qmd#movement-between-places)), given with the places as `stratify(patch=ss.levels(towns, mobility=...))`. Here are three towns of measles: Riverton, with 60,000 people, Hillside (30,000) 20 km away, and Lakeside (10,000) 50 km away, with 10 infectious people in Riverton at the start. People spend 0.1% of their time in the other towns, split between them by a gravity model (more to bigger and nearer towns):

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
import starsim as ss

towns = ss.geo.geography(
    names       = ['Riverton', 'Hillside', 'Lakeside'],
    populations = [60_000, 30_000, 10_000],
    x           = [0, 20, 50], # Positions in km
    y           = [0, 0, 10],
)

S, R = ss.states('S R')
I = ss.State('I', infected=True) # Infected: counted in the results infected and prevalence
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0]))) # 10 infectious people in Riverton
measles.stratify(patch=ss.levels(towns, mobility=ss.geo.gravity(away=0.001)))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, stop=ss.days(60))
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.I.by('patch').plot()
```

## R

```r
library(starsim)

towns <- ss$geo$geography(
  names       = c("Riverton", "Hillside", "Lakeside"),
  populations = c(60000, 30000, 10000),
  x           = c(0, 20, 50), # Positions in km
  y           = c(0, 0, 10)
)

states("S R")
states("I", infected = TRUE) # Infected: counted in the results infected and prevalence
measles <- Disease(
  infection = Transition(S, I, rate = 1.9 * I), # β = 1.9 per day
  recovery  = Transition(I, R, dur = days(8)),  # Infectious for 8 days on average
  init_n    = list(I = ss$by(patch = c(10, 0, 0)))  # 10 infectious people in Riverton
)
measles$stratify(patch = ss$levels(towns, mobility = ss$geo$gravity(away = 0.001)))

sim <- Sim(measles, stop = days(60))
sim$run()
sim$results$measles$I$by("patch")$plot()
```
:::

The sim takes its population (100,000) from the geography. Each town has its own epidemic, a few days after the one before: Hillside, which is bigger and nearer, before Lakeside. Without `mobility=`, people mix only within their own town, and the outbreak stays in Riverton:

```{python}
isolated = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0])), name='measles')
isolated.stratify(patch=towns) # The same towns, with no movement between them

no_movement = ss.Sim(isolated, stop=ss.days(60), verbose=0)
no_movement.run()
print('Infections with movement:')
print(sim.results.measles.infection.by('patch').summarize().round())
print('Infections without movement:')
print(no_movement.results.measles.infection.by('patch').summarize().round())
```

Even 0.1% of people's time spent away is enough to carry measles, with an R0 of 15, to every town; a disease with a lower R0 needs more movement to spread, and arrives later.

## Geographies

A geography can be given by hand, read from a file, or looked up by country:

```python
ss.geo.geography(names=['a', 'b'], populations=[10_000, 20_000], x=[0, 30], y=[0, 0])  # Positions in any unit of distance
ss.geo.geography(names=['a', 'b'], populations=[10_000, 20_000], lat=[-1.3, -0.1], lon=[36.8, 34.8]) # Latitudes and longitudes; distances in km
ss.geo.geography(names=['a', 'b'], populations=[10_000, 20_000], distances=[[0, 30], [30, 0]])   # Distances directly
ss.geo.geography('districts.csv')               # A table with columns name, pop, and x and y (or lat and lon)
ss.geo.geography('districts.shp')               # Shapes (.shp, .geojson, or .gpkg, read with geopandas); each place at the center of its shape
ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1)              # Kenya's 47 counties, with populations and positions
ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1, places=['Nairobi', 'Kiambu']) # Some of them
ss.geo.geography(['Kenya', 'Uganda'], level=1)  # Several countries, with places named e.g. 'Kenya:Busia'
ss.geo.geography(['Kenya', 'Uganda', 'Tanzania'], level=0) # Each country as one place
ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=2)              # The units below the counties (downloaded the first time)
ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1, year=2010)   # The counties' populations in another year (downloaded the first time)
```

A country's administrative units come from `starsim_data`: level 0 is the country itself, level 1 its counties, provinces, or states, and level 2 the units below them. Levels 0 and 1 are bundled for 184 countries and territories, so they need no download; level 2, and populations for a year other than 2020, are downloaded the first time (level 2 needs the optional package geopandas: `pip install starsim_data[spatial]`). The places that have units, and how many, are listed in the [appendix](#appendix-every-place-and-its-data). Each unit comes with its population, position, area (`kenya.area`, in km²), and p-code (`kenya.codes`, e.g. `'KE047'` for Nairobi), the standard code of an administrative unit, which is the reliable way to join surveillance data reported by unit to the places of a model, since names are spelled in different ways.

Here measles starts in Nairobi and spreads across Kenya's counties, in a population that is 90% immune (as from vaccination), so that R0 = 15 gives an effective reproduction number of about 1.5:

```{python}
kenya = ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1)

measles_kenya = ss.Disease(infection, recovery,
    init   = dict(R=0.9),                         # 90% immune at the start
    init_n = dict(I=ss.by(patch={'Nairobi': 10})), # 10 infectious people in Nairobi, and none in the other 46 counties
)
measles_kenya.stratify(patch=ss.levels(kenya, mobility=ss.geo.gravity(away=0.001)))

sim = ss.Sim(measles_kenya, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01', verbose=0)
sim.run()
res = sim.results.measles_kenya
for county in ['Nairobi', 'Kiambu', 'Mombasa', 'Turkana']:
    peak = res.I.select(patch=county).values.argmax()
    print(county, '- infectious people peak on', res.timevec[peak])
```

Kiambu borders Nairobi, Mombasa is the second city, 440 km away, and Turkana is a remote county in the northwest. Nairobi's outbreak peaks first, in June; Kiambu's follows in July, and Mombasa's and Turkana's in September, near the peaks of most other counties. The gravity model sends Nairobi's travelers to every county, near or far, in proportion to its population, so distance matters less than it might: Turkana, remote as it is, peaks within days of Mombasa. As an ODE, a county's outbreak starts as soon as the first fraction of an infected person arrives (see [below](#under-compartments-and-agents) for why agents differ).

A geography with no populations (`names=` only) gives places of equal size. A place's population sets the share of people who start there.

## Maps

A result of a model stratified by place can be drawn on a map of the places, with the result's `map()`. Each place is colored by the result there, and drawn as its shape, if the geography has shapes, or else as a point at its position, with an area in proportion to its population. Since places differ in size, a share, such as the prevalence, usually shows the spread better than a count. `shapes=True` draws a country's units as their boundaries, which are downloaded the first time (this needs geopandas: `pip install starsim_data[spatial]`). Here is the outbreak above, on the first of May, July, and September:

```{python}
res.prevalence.map(t=['2025-05-01', '2025-07-01', '2025-09-01'], shapes=True)
```

In May, the outbreak is in Nairobi alone; by July it has spread to the counties around it, and by September, when it is over in Nairobi, it is at its height across the rest of the country. The options:

| Call | What it draws |
|---|---|
| `res.map()` | One map of the result's summary in each place over the run, as `summarize()` gives it (the total of a flow, the mean of a ratio, the final value of a stock) |
| `res.map(n=6)` | Six maps, evenly spaced from the start of the outbreak to its end |
| `res.map(t='2025-02-01')` | The map on one date, or on each of a list of dates (or times, e.g. `t=[15, 25]`, for a sim without dates) |
| `res.map(animate=True)` | An animation, shown in a notebook with controls to play it; elsewhere, it is returned as a Matplotlib animation |
| `res.map(animate=True, filename='spread.gif')` | The same, saved to a file (a GIF, or an MP4, which needs ffmpeg) |
| `res.map(shapes=True)` | For a country, its units' boundaries, downloaded the first time (this needs geopandas: `pip install starsim_data[spatial]`); a geography read from shapes always draws them |
| `geo.plot()` | The places of a geography, with their populations |
| `geo.plot(values=..., label=...)` | The places colored by a value for each one, in order or by name, e.g. a summary of a result: `kenya.plot(values=res.infection.by('patch').summarize()/kenya.populations, label='Share infected')` |

Both take `cmap=` (the colors, by default from white to red), `vmin=` and `vmax=` (the range of the color scale), and `names=` (whether to label the places, by default when there are 15 or fewer). A result of agents is mapped the same way; for the runs of a MultiSim, map one run (`res.select(run=0)`).

## Values by place

Anything that can vary by level of a stratification can vary by place, with `ss.by(patch=...)`: a value for each place, in order, or a dict by name. Above, `init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0]))` starts the outbreak in one place, as does `ss.by(patch={'Riverton': 10})`: in a starting value (`init`, `init_n`, or `init_prev`), a place left out of a dict starts with 0, while a rate or other parameter by name needs every place, since a missing one there is more likely a mistake; a transmission rate by place is `S >> I @ ss.by(patch=[1.9, 1.9, 1.0])*I`. Results are by place too: `by('patch')` splits a result into one column for each place, and `select()` picks one, e.g. `sim.results.measles.I.select(patch='Hillside')`. Contact matrices act within each place, so a model can be stratified by age and by place together, with a contact matrix by age (see [Mixing](populations_mixing.qmd#a-contact-matrix-by-age)).

## Under compartments and agents

Places and movement work the same under every solver: with agents, each agent has a home place, and commuting and visiting weight its exposure by where it spends its time. Where they differ is in how infection first reaches a place. In an ODE, a tiny fraction of an infected person in a town starts its epidemic growing at once; with agents, a whole person there has to be infected first, which takes longer, and by chance may not happen at all. With less movement than above, the difference is large:

```{python}
measles_slow = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0])))
measles_slow.stratify(patch=ss.levels(towns, mobility=ss.geo.gravity(away=0.0001)))

kw = dict(stop=ss.days(60), verbose=0)
for label, sim in {'As an ODE': ss.Sim(measles_slow, **kw), 'As agents': ss.Sim(measles_slow, n_agents=10_000, **kw)}.items():
    sim.run()
    peaks = sim.results.measles_slow.I.by('patch').values.argmax(axis=0)
    print(label, '- day of the peak in Riverton, Hillside, and Lakeside:', peaks)
```

As an ODE, Hillside and Lakeside peak 3 or 4 days after Riverton; as agents, 7 and 13 days after. (Riverton itself peaks later as agents too, for reasons that have nothing to do with places: its outbreak starts from one agent, who stands for the 10 infectious people, and agents take steps of a day, which is long for measles; see [Solvers and backends](running_solvers.qmd).) For questions about whether, or when, an outbreak reaches a small place, agents (or a stochastic compartmental model: see [Solvers and backends](running_solvers.qmd)) give the better answer; for the size of an epidemic across places that are all well seeded, an ODE is enough.

## Pitfalls

- **A name does not make a place.** A stratification is spatial when it is given a geography (`patch=towns`) or `kind='space'` (`stratify(patch=ss.levels(['a', 'b'], kind='space'))`). A list of names alone, even `patch=['north', 'south']`, makes ordinary groups, whose people mix with each other; a stratification named like places (`patch`, `region`, `district`, `county`, `province`, `place`, or `location`) given only names says so in a note, unless `kind=` is given. `describe()` gives the kind of each stratification: `patch (space)` or `patch (plain)`.
- **Start the outbreak somewhere.** `init_prev=0.01` infects 1% of people in every place; to start it in one place, give `init_n` (or `init`) by place, e.g. `init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch={'Nairobi': 10}))`.
- **Check the links.** Before trusting a spatial model, seed one place and check that the others stay free of infection with no movement (as [above](#towns-linked-by-commuting)), and that with migration, the population of each place changes as it should. With agents that each stand for several people, the number of people who move and the number of agents who move are not the same.
- **Strata multiply.** Every place multiplies the number of compartments: 47 counties × 16 age groups × 3 states is 2,256 compartments. An ODE handles that easily, but results by group take memory, and a model can grow large by accident; `describe()` lists each stratification with its levels.
- **Check the data's units and years.** A contact survey gives contacts a day, a crude birth rate is per 1,000 people a year, and the data don't all have the same reference year; record the source and year with an analysis.

The API reference for this page: [ss.data](../api/data.qmd), [ss.geo](../api/geo.qmd).

## Further reading

- [UN World Population Prospects](https://population.un.org/wpp/): the populations, birth rates, and death rates that come with Starsim
- [epydemix: Populations](https://epydemix.readthedocs.io/en/latest/guide/populations.html): populations and contact matrices by place, for compartmental models
- [flepiMoP: Model description](https://iddynamics.gitbook.io/flepimop/gempyor/model-description): metapopulation models of US states and counties, with mobility between them
- [MEmilio: Metapopulation models](https://memilio.readthedocs.io/en/latest/cpp/metapop.html): compartmental models of regions joined by commuting

## Appendix: what a geography has

The attributes of a geography (`kenya = ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1)`), for making maps, movement matrices of your own, or joining data by place:

| Attribute | What it is |
|---|---|
| `names` | The name of each place, in order: the levels of the stratification |
| `populations` | The population of each place (None if not given) |
| `lat`, `lon` | The latitude and longitude of each place, in degrees (for a country's units, the center of each unit) |
| `x`, `y` | The positions of the places, for a geography given by hand with `x=` and `y=` |
| `distances` | The distance between each pair of places (in km, from latitudes and longitudes) |
| `adjacency` | Whether each pair of places shares a border (for a country's units at level 1 or below, or as given) |
| `area` | The area of each place, in km² (for a country's units) |
| `codes` | The p-code of each place (for a country's units), e.g. `'KE047'` |
| `shapes` | The shapes of the places, for a geography read from shapes (None otherwise; `res.map(shapes=True)` downloads a country's) |
| `ref` | Where a country's units came from, which `describe()` shows |

`len(kenya)` is the number of places, and `kenya.plot()` draws them (see [Maps](#maps)).

## Appendix: every dataset

The datasets of `starsim_data`, with how each is reached: bundled with the package, fetched (downloaded on first use from the files published with it), or downloaded from the original source (here, the UN), and the number of places each has:

```{python}
datasets = ssd.list_datasets(detailed=True)
datasets[['dataset', 'description', 'access', 'locations']]
```

The contact matrices (`prem2021`, `prem2017`, `prem`, `mistry2021`, and, for US states, `mistry2021_us`) are the `study=` of `ss.contacts()` and `ss.data.contacts()`. Those of Prem et al. are by 5-year age group, from 0-4 to 75+; those of Mistry et al. by single year of age, from 0 to 84+. Each has the settings `'home'`, `'school'`, `'work'`, and `'community'` (`layer=`), and their sum, `'all'`. The administrative units at level 2 and below are not in a dataset of their own: `ss.geo.geography(place, level=2)` downloads the boundaries (from geoBoundaries or UN OCHA, where they have that level for the place) and the populations, and needs the optional geopandas (`pip install starsim_data[spatial]`). `indicators` and `life_table` are the UN's other tables, which `ssd.download(place, which='life_table')` gives.

## Appendix: every place and its data

Every place that has data, with its ISO code, the contact matrices it has, and its number of first-level administrative units (blank where there are none bundled). Every place listed has the UN's population, birth, death, fertility, and migration data:

```{python}
import pandas as pd

places = ssd.list_all_locations()
sources = ['prem2021', 'prem2017', 'mistry2021']
has = {source: set(ssd.list_locations(source)) for source in sources}
with_units = set(ssd.list_locations('nodes'))
un_data = all(set(ssd.list_locations(ds)) == set(places) for ds in ['population', 'births', 'deaths', 'fertility', 'migration'])
print('Every place has all the UN data:', un_data)

rows = []
for place in places:
    row = dict(place=place.replace('_', ' '), code=ssd.location_info(place).iso3)
    row['contact matrices'] = ', '.join(source for source in sources if place in has[source])
    row['level-1 units'] = len(ssd.load_nodes(place, level=1)) if place in with_units else None
    rows.append(row)
table = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('place')
table['level-1 units'] = table['level-1 units'].astype('Int64')
print(len(table), 'places')
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The table of places"}
```{python}
pd.set_option('display.max_rows', 250)
table
```
:::

US states are named with their country, e.g. `'United States:Massachusetts'`, and have their own populations (from the US Census) and contact matrices (Mistry et al.); `ssd.list_locations('population_us')` lists them.
